source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Core idea. Replace the objective with a score for how different a behaviour is from the current population and an archive of past novel behaviours. Novelty is the mean distance to the k nearest neighbours in behaviour space. An individual enters the permanent archive if its novelty passes a threshold.
numbers: NEAT settings: k=15 nearest neighbours; archive threshold starts at 6.0 (maze) and 1.0 (biped); population 250.
limits: The behaviour space and distance are hand-written per domain.
agent_relevance: Maps to a code-computed idea descriptor plus a distance. The archive entry rule is a counted rule, not a model judgement (fits the schema rule that code decides).

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Medium maze: both novelty and objective search solved it in every run, but novelty was about 3x faster. Random selection solved it in only 21 of 40 runs, so the gain is not just random wandering.
numbers: Novelty 18,274 evals (sd 20,447) vs fitness NEAT 56,334 (sd 48,705), 40 runs each, p<0.001 t-test. Random selection: 21/40 runs solved. Solutions: 24.6 connections (novelty) vs 66.74 (fitness).
limits: One simulated robot-maze family, 40 runs per arm.
agent_relevance: Baseline effect size for novelty vs objective on a mildly deceptive task: roughly 3x fewer evaluations.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Hard (deceptive) maze: the objective (distance to goal) is no better than random; novelty almost always solves it. This is the clean demonstration that a deceptive objective can block its own goal.
numbers: Fitness NEAT solved 3/40 runs; random selection 4/40; novelty 39/40, mean 35,109 evals (sd 30,236), 250,000-eval cap.
quote: the same NEAT algorithm can almost never solve it when solving the maze is made the explicit objective, yet solves it almost every time
limits: Maze deception is built by hand. Real problems rarely announce their deception.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: novelty pressure pays only when the progress signal misleads. On non-deceptive tasks keep objective pressure (supports G1: switch on a signal, not a schedule).

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: The archive can be bounded. Limiting it to the population size (250) did not hurt on the hard maze.
numbers: 40 runs, all solved, 38,324 evals (sd 42,229); not significantly different from unbounded.
limits: Shown on one maze. Dropped behaviours may become unreachable.
agent_relevance: A small bounded archive of idea cells is enough in this domain; supports a cheap history state (S3).

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: The behaviour characterisation can be very coarse. Discretising the maze end point to a grid still let novelty search solve the hard maze, except for the smallest grids.
numbers: 960 runs; only 4 failed within 500,000 evals. A 4x4 grid (16 behaviours) needed 117,107 evals on average, about 3x slower than the original, still better than fitness search.
limits: Only the maze; the descriptor (end point) is well aligned with the task.
agent_relevance: A crude descriptor of an idea (a few categories) may be enough. Around 16 cells or fewer hurt.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Biped walking: novelty search evolved farther walkers than distance-fitness search and avoided the deceptive local optimum of a few steps then falling.
numbers: 50 runs. Novelty mean 4.04 m (sd 2.57) vs fitness 2.88 m (sd 1.04), p<0.01. Best gait 13.7 m vs 6.8 m. 80% of novelty runs found oscillatory gaits; over 40% of fitness runs converged on non-oscillatory gaits.
limits: The mean gain is modest; the best-case gain is large.
agent_relevance: Novelty helps the tail (best of many), not only the mean. Matches use of a diverse pool for best-of-N.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: The authors name the limit themselves: novelty search finds approximate solutions well, and objective optimisation is good for tuning them. They suggest combining the two. Archive nearest-neighbour cost grows with archive size.
quote: novelty search effectively finds approximate solutions, while objective optimization is good for tuning approximate solutions
limits: Argument in the discussion, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Supports explore then exploit: novelty-driven candidate generation, then objective-driven repair from real failing output (G2).

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: MAP-Elites algorithm. The user picks 2 or more feature dimensions, discretised into a grid. Each cell keeps only its best solution. Loop: pick a random filled cell, mutate its elite, measure features and performance, replace the cell occupant if the child is better or the cell is empty. Called an illumination algorithm.
numbers: Needs only a feature function, a performance function, a mutation operator and a grid.
limits: Grid size grows exponentially with the number of feature dimensions. Features must be chosen by the designer.
agent_relevance: Simplest implementable QD: a dictionary from descriptor tuple to best attempt, random parent from filled cells. Code-only.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: Retina (deceptive neural-network) experiment: MAP-Elites beat three controls (traditional EA, novelty search with local competition, random sampling) on all four criteria, including the single best solution.
numbers: 20 independent runs per treatment, equal evaluations, p<1e-7 on global performance, reliability, precision and coverage. Random sampling was second best on coverage.
limits: Normalised scores are in figures; exact per-arm values not printed in text. Retina task is stylised and deceptive.
agent_relevance: Even when only the best answer matters, filling many cells can beat a pure optimiser on deceptive problems. Random sampling already gives decent coverage, so a diversity method must beat it.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: Lineage analysis: most elites descend from nearby cells, but many high performers descend from a good neighbour a medium distance away. Whole lineages cross many regions of the map. This is the stepping-stone evidence.
numbers: No sampled organism came from a parent more than halfway across the map.
limits: One domain (retina); descriptive.
agent_relevance: Keep weak ideas in other cells: they may be parents of later strong ideas. Argues against keeping only the top-k.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: Soft robot morphologies: within one ordinary evolutionary run most morphologies were similar and stuck on one peak, while one MAP-Elites run produced many locomotion types.
limits: Qualitative comparison with earlier work; no sample sizes for that remark.
agent_relevance: A single optimiser run collapses to one idea family; our agent needs an explicit archive to avoid this.

source: Fontaine, Togelius, Nikolaidis, Hoover (2020) Covariance Matrix Adaptation for the Rapid Illumination of Behavior Space (CMA-ME)
finding: Adding a self-adapting optimiser (CMA-ES emitters) to the MAP-Elites archive fills more cells and reaches higher quality on continuous problems. Plain CMA-ES (pure optimisation) fills almost none of the map.
numbers: Sphere n=20, cells occupied: CMA-ES 3.46%, MAP-Elites 56.22%, ME(line) 68.99%, CMA-ME(rd) 90.32%, CMA-ME(imp) 87.75%. n=100: 3.74%, 26.97%, 31.75%, 77.12%, 61.98%. 2.5M evals per run.
limits: Toy sphere and Rastrigin; the CMA-ME(opt) emitter did badly (12.5% and 2.7% cells).
agent_relevance: QD is strongest when parent choice adapts to what filled new cells. Analogue: an operator selector rewarded for filling an empty cell (link to the bandits subfield).

source: Fontaine et al. (2020) CMA-ME
finding: Hearthstone deck search: CMA-ME got more than double the QD-score of MAP-Elites and a higher win rate for the best deck. Authors suspect the objective is a deceptive trap for CMA-ES here.
limits: One game, one descriptor pair (e.g. hand size).
agent_relevance: Diversity machinery raised the best-solution quality too, not only coverage, on a deceptive objective.

source: Pugh, Soros, Stanley (2016) Quality diversity: a new frontier for evolutionary computation
finding: Defines quality diversity: return a set of niches each filled with as good a solution as possible, diversity first and quality second. Compares novelty search with local competition (NSLC: quality ranked only among k=20 behavioural neighbours) and MAP-Elites variants.
numbers: 15 algorithm/behaviour-characterisation combinations, 20 runs each, 900 runs, three simulated maze tasks (250k to 1M evals).
limits: Read through a fetch summary of the first 100k of 145k characters.
agent_relevance: Vocabulary and metrics for our archive: QD-score = sum of best quality per niche; coverage; whether the descriptor is aligned with quality.

source: Pugh, Soros, Stanley (2016) Quality diversity: a new frontier for evolutionary computation
finding: Alignment matters. A behaviour descriptor aligned with the goal (end point) beat the plain objective on hard mazes. A descriptor unaligned with the goal (facing direction) did worse than the objective at finding solutions; on the symmetric gauntlet only one variant found any.
numbers: Aligned (EndpointBC) treatments beat Fitness at p<0.001. Unaligned (DirectionBC) worse than Fitness at p<0.05; symmetric gauntlet: only MEPGD_d found solutions, 2 of 20 runs.
limits: Three mazes, simulated wheeled robot only; authors say results show potential differences, no multiple-comparison correction, several differences not significant (NSLC_e vs NS_e p=0.093).
agent_relevance: Key boundary: diversity along an irrelevant axis does not escape deception. The idea descriptor must relate to what makes answers right.

source: Pugh, Soros, Stanley (2016) Quality diversity: a new frontier for evolutionary computation
finding: Using an aligned and an unaligned descriptor together balanced solution-finding and diversity. MAP-Elites with a second slot per bin that accepts worse individuals 30% of the time (MEPGD) beat plain MAP-Elites on both gauntlets.
numbers: Multi-BC NS_eNSLC_d tied NSLC_e on symmetric-gauntlet QD-score (p=0.163). MEPGD_e beat ME_e on both gauntlets (significant).
limits: Concatenating descriptors was not tested; three mazes.
agent_relevance: Two descriptors (one tied to task success, one for style) is a workable archive design.

source: Kistemaker & Whiteson (2011) Critical factors in the performance of novelty search
finding: Independent analysis of what makes novelty search work. Performance depends strongly on the behaviour function. Removing irrelevant behaviour dimensions speeds search sharply. Grouping genotypes with different descendant-fitness chances into one behaviour slows it.
numbers: 70 runs per setting, cap 2e6 evaluations. With 3 behaviour points 21 of 70 runs failed to find the optimum; with 4 points 29 of 70 failed.
quote: the design of a good behavior function is essential to novelty search's success
limits: Toy grid worlds plus three deceptive mazes. In the hard maze a larger characterisation made no difference; in the star maze it helped.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition rather than refutation: the headline result is conditional on a good descriptor. Descriptor design is the cost.

source: Kistemaker & Whiteson (2011) Critical factors in the performance of novelty search
finding: Authors conclude novelty search still relies on prior knowledge, in the behaviour function instead of the fitness function. Finding a good behaviour function may be as hard as solving the problem.
quote: finding a good behavior function may be as difficult as solving the optimization problem itself
limits: Opinion drawn from small domains.
agent_relevance: No free lunch from novelty. Test the descriptor on held-out tasks before trusting it (G3).

source: Cully, Clune, Tarapore, Mouret (2015) Robots that can adapt like animals
finding: A MAP-Elites map built in simulation (about 13,000 hexapod gaits over a 6-D contact-pattern space) is a prior for fast on-robot adaptation. After damage the robot tries map entries guided by Bayesian optimisation and recovers in minutes.
numbers: 240 main hexapod experiments (6 conditions x 5 runs x 8 maps). Adapted vs reference speed: leg missing 0.21 vs 0.04 m/s; unpowered leg 0.22 vs 0.03; two legs missing 0.17 vs 0.05. Damaged cases median 66 s and 8 trials; the 20-trial cap hit in 2 of 240. Map build: 40M iterations, about two weeks. Standard Bayesian optimisation in raw parameter space found no working controller.
limits: Read through a fetch summary (first 100k of 169k characters). Needs a simulator and two weeks of compute.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that an archive of diverse good solutions is reusable as a prior when conditions change. Analogue: stored solution patterns reused on a related problem.

source: Cully, Clune, Tarapore, Mouret (2015) Robots that can adapt like animals
finding: Same method on a simulated 8-joint planar arm: 14 damage conditions each repeated 15 times (210 runs); adaptation usually under 30 seconds and fewer than 10 trials, with a 20,000-cell map (200x100) from 20 million evaluations.
numbers: 210 runs; 2-D behaviour space; 8 controller parameters.
limits: Simulated arm only.
agent_relevance: A low-dimensional descriptor (2-D) was enough for a useful prior.

source: Lehman, Gordon, Jain, Ndousse, Yeh, Stanley (2022) Evolution through Large Models (ELM)
finding: An LLM trained on code diffs works as a mutation operator inside MAP-Elites. In a bug-fixing test, one LLM mutation can fix several coupled bugs at once, where random GP mutation fails exponentially.
numbers: 4-Parity with 0 to 5 injected bugs: GP mutation success falls exponentially and is zero at five bugs; the 300M diff model degrades only at the fifth bug.
limits: Success percentages read from a log-scale figure; one toy task.
agent_relevance: The model is the mutation slot; code is the selector and archive keeper.

source: Lehman, Gordon, Jain, Ndousse, Yeh, Stanley (2022) Evolution through Large Models (ELM)
finding: Sodarace: ELM with MAP-Elites over 1,728 niches (height, width, mass) from one seed program filled most niches. Fine-tuning the diff model on accepted diffs raised QD-score and the share of valid and runnable diffs. Seed choice mattered: Square seed filled high-mass niches slowly; CPPN seed gave diversity fastest; Radial seed gave higher quality but chaotic programs.
numbers: 1,024,000 evaluations per run (2,000 iterations x 512 diffs); three runs per seed; later datasets: 280K examples at a 50% per-niche cutoff, 95K at 80%.
limits: Three runs per seed; exact fill percentages only in figures. Chaotic Radial-seed data harmed downstream training.
agent_relevance: Diverse data plus a per-niche quality threshold makes good pools. The first idea strongly shapes the archive (seed sensitivity).

source: Lehman, Gordon, Jain, Ndousse, Yeh, Stanley (2022) Evolution through Large Models (ELM)
finding: Quality-versus-diversity dial when distilling the archive: a stricter per-niche cutoff (80%) gave less diverse but higher-quality data than a looser one (50%), and models trained on it reflected that. The stage-3 conditional RL model matched the dataset at 80% and improved on it at 50%.
numbers: Datasets 95K (80%) vs 280K (50%) examples; 1,024 samples per model for evaluation.
limits: Single domain.
agent_relevance: An explicit dial that code can set: keep attempts above a percentage of the best in each cell.

source: Bradley, Dai, Teufel, Zhang, Oostermeijer, Bellagente, Clune, Stanley, Schott, Lehman (2023) Quality-Diversity through AI Feedback (QDAIF)
finding: QDAIF: the LLM both mutates text and, by prompted feedback, scores quality and places each text in a diversity bin (genre, ending sentiment). A MAP-Elites archive does the rest. QDAIF got significantly higher QD-score than non-QD baselines in all text domains tested.
numbers: 2,000 iterations, 5 seeds, bootstrapped 95% CI from 100k resamples. Maximum QD score 20 for 1-D archives and 100 for the 2-D archive. Baselines: Fixed-Few-Shot, Shuffling-Few-Shot, Random-Search, LMX Quality-Only.
limits: Per-method QD values are in a figure. Domains are short opinions and stories.
agent_relevance: Direct template for the history state: LLM labels the idea cell, code keeps the archive and picks an empty or weak cell next.

source: Bradley, Dai, Teufel, Zhang, Oostermeijer, Bellagente, Clune, Stanley, Schott, Lehman (2023) Quality-Diversity through AI Feedback (QDAIF)
finding: Human check: QDAIF samples were competitive with or better than baselines, but a fixed few-shot prompt was almost as good on human QD score and higher on human quality rating. Human-AI agreement on labels was highest for QDAIF.
numbers: Table 1 averaged over three domains: Human QD score QDAIF 0.772, Fixed-Few-Shot 0.767, Shuffling-Few-Shot 0.696, LMX Quality-Only 0.650, Random-Search 0.606. Human-AI agreement QDAIF 0.833, Fixed 0.800, Random 0.733. Human quality rating: Fixed-Few-Shot 4.133 vs QDAIF 3.900.
limits: Small study; annotators were co-authors and colleagues.
agent_relevance: The human-measured gain over a good fixed-prompt baseline is tiny (0.772 vs 0.767). Do not expect large wins from archive logic alone; measure it.

source: Bradley, Dai, Teufel, Zhang, Oostermeijer, Bellagente, Clune, Stanley, Schott, Lehman (2023) Quality-Diversity through AI Feedback (QDAIF)
finding: Reward hacking: AI quality scores track human quality, but the correlation breaks at the top of the scale. Search pushed texts toward phrasings the judge liked but humans did not.
numbers: Correlation drops for AI quality in the range 0.995 to 1. Annotators differed by 2 to 3 units in 15% and 5% of cases.
quote: the correlation drops when the evaluated quality is in the range 0.995 to 1
limits: Authors only suspect the mechanism.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema rule: the model must not grade itself without a check. Cap optimisation pressure against an LLM judge.

source: Bradley, Dai, Teufel, Zhang, Oostermeijer, Bellagente, Clune, Stanley, Schott, Lehman (2023) Quality-Diversity through AI Feedback (QDAIF)
finding: Poetry with GPT-4 as mutator and judge: QDAIF covered genres and tones better than random poem generation and a seed-rewrite control. Without genre guidance it failed to fill some bins (limericks). Adding guidance on target genre and tone matched a baseline that directly asks for a poem of a randomly chosen genre and tone.
numbers: 200 iterations; QD score 130 (CI 118-145) vs Random-Poems 76 (CI 67-85) vs Fixed Seed Rewrite 99 (CI 72-117); Mann-Whitney U p<=0.05.
limits: The directly targeted baseline matched the guided variant.
agent_relevance: Telling the model which empty cell to fill is as good as evolving toward it. Cheapest design: code names the empty cell in the prompt.

source: Zhang, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2023) OMNI: open-endedness via models of human notions of interestingness
finding: An LLM acts as a model of interestingness to pick which learnable tasks an RL agent practises next. It learned more tasks than uniform sampling and than learning-progress alone, and came close to an oracle of interestingness.
numbers: Crafter (100M steps, 10 seeds, median) tasks learned: uniform 4, learning progress 55, OMNI 82; interesting tasks learned 3, 9, 14. BabyAI: 1, 4, 8. AI2-THOR (1M steps), tasks with success >=0.6: 0, 2, 13.
limits: Read through a fetch summary. Boring tasks were built synthetically; very hard tasks assumed success 0; authors expect Goodhart effects if interestingness is optimised hard.
agent_relevance: An LLM-judged 'worth exploring' signal can filter the archive. Use as a hint for a filter step only.

source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2024) Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models (FunSearch), Nature
finding: FunSearch: an LLM writes program variants, an evaluator scores them, programs live on islands; every 4 hours the worst half of islands are reset from a surviving island. Prompts hold k=2 programs. It found a cap set of size 512 in n=8 and a better asymptotic cap set bound. Only 4 of 140 experiments found the 512 set, so it is high variance.
numbers: Capacity lower bound 2.2202 vs previous 2.2180. About 1e6 samples; 15 samplers, 150 CPU evaluators. Bin packing excess bins: OR4 2.47% vs best-fit 4.94%; Weibull 100k 0.03% vs 3.79%.
limits: Read through a fetch summary. Ablations of islands and diversity are in the supplement and were not read.
agent_relevance: Islands plus reset are a cheap guard against all attempts collapsing onto one family. Many runs matter because success per run was low.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve: a coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
finding: AlphaEvolve extends FunSearch to whole files and multiple objectives. Its program database mixes MAP-Elites with island models to balance exploring and exploiting. On over 50 open maths problems it matched the best known on 75% and beat it on 20%. It found a rank-48 algorithm for 4x4 complex matrix multiplication.
numbers: 14 matrix-multiplication targets improved; kissing number in 11 dimensions improved (593 spheres); a scheduling heuristic recovers on average 0.7% of Google fleet compute.
limits: No ablation isolates the MAP-Elites/diversity part of the database.
agent_relevance: Industrial proof that archive-based LLM search works when a code evaluator exists. Our agent lacks a cheap evaluator on open tasks, so the benefit is limited to checkable problems.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve: a coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
finding: Ablations on tensor decomposition and kissing numbers: removing evolution (feeding the same initial program repeatedly) lowers the result at equal compute. Removing prompt context, meta-prompt evolution or full-file evolution, or using only a small base LLM, each also hurt.
numbers: Averages over targets, three seeds per setting, curves against fraction of compute budget; values only in Figure 8.
limits: The evolution ablation is 'no database at all', not 'database without diversity'. It cannot show that the quality-diversity part is what matters.
agent_relevance: Reusing earlier attempts beats fresh resampling at equal budget. Archive diversity itself is untested: put in the test backlog.

source: Stanley & Lehman (2015) Why greatness cannot be planned: the myth of the objective (book)
finding: Popular statement of the theory: ambitious goals are deceptive, so collecting interesting and different stepping stones beats chasing the objective. Seen only in a search listing; not read.
limits: Not opened; no numbers used.
agent_relevance: Source of the stepping-stone rationale only; not evidence.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Evolving a diversity of virtual creatures through novelty search and local competition (GECCO)
finding: Origin of NSLC: novelty search where quality is ranked only against behavioural neighbours. Cited in MAP-Elites and Pugh as the main predecessor. Known only through citations.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Predecessor of the 'compare quality only within the same cell' rule.
